summary:
Consensual sexual intimacy between adults is not a criminal offence in Antigua and Barbuda. On 5 July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. The ruling struck down the country's buggery and gross indecency provisions, which Human Rights Watch described as the sodomy and gross indecency offences. The penalties those sections carried before the judgment were up to fifteen years' imprisonment for adult-on-adult buggery, five years where a minor committed the act, and life imprisonment where an adult committed it on a minor; serious indecency carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen; and a person convicted of buggery as a repeat offender was placed on the Sex Offenders Register for the remainder of their life.

The same judgment read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. That is an interpretive holding by the court and has not been translated into a statutory protection regime. Antiguan law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Outright International records that transgender people are particularly vulnerable in Antigua and Barbuda because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers, and only name changes are available. For a trans visitor this is the operative constraint: a change of the sex recorded on identity documents is not possible in the country, by administrative or judicial route, so travel documents and any local identity check will continue to show the sex assigned at birth.

No form of same-sex union is recognised in Antigua and Barbuda, and households headed by such couples are not eligible for the rights granted to married opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor travelling with a partner whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no route to have that relationship recognised during the stay.

Decriminalisation followed years of official resistance. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review of the UN Human Rights Council, Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua urged the government to repeal its sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people. Minister of Social Transformation Samantha Marshall described the ban as antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman told the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. On 24 August 2016 the government announced it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would almost certainly strike it down given the identical jurisprudence already established in Belize.

On 1 November 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced it would file a legal challenge, which culminated in the 5 July 2022 ruling. The group's stated argument was that buggery and indecency laws stigmatise LGBT people and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence. The litigant, Orden David, had been bullied and physically attacked before bringing the case, including being struck in the head and knocked unconscious in daylight.

The Advocates for Human Rights filed a submission with the UN Human Rights Committee in January 2025, ahead of that body's review of Antigua and Barbuda, listing LGBTQ+ rights issues that remain open following decriminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda's 2022 ruling sits inside a regional litigation campaign. The Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced or filed challenges in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, and reporting in June 2023 recorded that six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct. Travel within the eastern Caribbean therefore crosses jurisdictions holding materially different positions: Antigua and Barbuda has decriminalised, while the same conduct remains an offence on neighbouring islands.

The comparison that drove Antiguan official expectations in 2016 was Belize, where an identical provision had already been struck down, rather than any domestic legislative choice.
localsOnly:
For residents the practical effects of the 2022 judgment are narrower than the decriminalisation headline. Antiguan law does not address discrimination or harassment on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, so neither is a protected ground in employment, housing or service provision. No form of same-sex union is recognised, and a household headed by a couple read locally as same-sex is ineligible for the benefits available to married opposite-sex couples. Transgender residents cannot amend the sex recorded on their identity documents; only a name change is available.

People convicted as repeat offenders of buggery before 2022 were placed on the Sex Offenders Register for the remainder of their life, and successive governments publicly resisted repeal until the court acted.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports trans-specific violence figures for Antigua and Barbuda, and none gives the country's general homicide rate, so no comparison between the two can be made. The inventory records one assault on a named activist before the 2022 litigation; it is a single incident and cannot be read as a rate.

Police and immigration practice toward trans visitors, including document screening and any differential treatment in custody or at ports of entry, is not addressed in the inventory.

It is unresolved whether convictions entered under Sections 12 and 15 before the 2022 judgment have been expunged, and what has become of the lifetime Sex Offenders Register entries imposed on repeat offenders. No source addresses this.

Whether the court's reading of sex discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity has been applied in any later case, tribunal or administrative decision is not sourced.

The January 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee is described only at the level of its subject matter; the specific issues it raises are not itemised in the inventory.
